items.title: Octopuses have three hearts
items.summary: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and a third pumps it around the body. Their blood is blue because it uses copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.

items.title: Tardigrades survived open space
items.summary: In 2007 tardigrades flown on the FOTON-M3 mission survived exposure to the vacuum of space, and some survived the added solar radiation. They can enter a dried-out state that lets them endure extremes.

items.title: The Antikythera mechanism
items.summary: A corroded bronze device recovered from a Greek shipwreck turned out to be a geared calculator for predicting astronomical positions and eclipses. It is often described as the oldest known analogue computer.

items.title: The Voyager Golden Record
items.summary: Both Voyager probes carry a gold-plated record of sounds, music and greetings from Earth, with instructions for playing it etched on the cover. The probes are now in interstellar space.

items.title: The Great Molasses Flood
items.summary: In January 1919 a huge storage tank burst in Boston's North End and sent a wave of molasses through the streets, killing 21 people. Locals said the area smelled of molasses for decades.

items.title: Methuselah, a tree over 4,800 years old
items.summary: A Great Basin bristlecone pine in California's White Mountains is among the oldest known non-clonal trees. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it.

items.title: The Voynich manuscript
items.summary: A fifteenth-century illustrated book written in an unknown script has resisted every attempt at decipherment. Its plants, star charts and bathing figures remain unexplained.

items.title: The dancing plague of 1518
items.summary: In Strasbourg in 1518 a woman began dancing in the street and dozens of others joined over the following weeks. Historians still debate what caused it.

items.title: The Lascaux cave paintings
items.summary: Teenagers exploring a cave in south-western France in 1940 found hundreds of painted animals estimated at around 17,000 years old. The original cave is closed to protect the paintings; visitors see replicas.

items.title: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault
items.summary: Deep inside a mountain on a Norwegian Arctic island, a vault stores backup copies of seeds from gene banks around the world. In 2015 it made its first withdrawal, to replace collections lost in Syria.

items.title: The Ig Nobel Prizes
items.summary: Each year the Ig Nobel Prizes honour real research that first makes people laugh, then makes them think. Winners have studied things like why woodpeckers don't get headaches.

items.title: The Mpemba effect
items.summary: The claim that hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water is named after a Tanzanian student who raised it in 1963. Whether it really happens, and why, is still disputed.

items.title: Kintsugi, the art of golden repair
items.summary: Kintsugi is the Japanese practice of mending broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold. The repair is meant to be seen, as part of the object's history.

items.title: The theremin, played without touching
items.summary: The theremin, invented by Leon Theremin in the 1920s, is played by moving your hands near two antennas. It gave many old science-fiction films their eerie sound.

items.title: A bank that accepts Parmesan as collateral
items.summary: Credito Emiliano, an Italian bank, has long accepted wheels of Parmigiano-Reggiano as collateral for loans to cheesemakers, ageing them in its own climate-controlled warehouses.

items.title: Crows remember human faces
items.summary: Researchers in Seattle wore masks while trapping crows and found the birds scolded that mask for years afterwards, and that other crows learned to scold it too.
